claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by lattice-distortion-induced sluggish diffusion.
An equiatomic TaNbHfZr-type alloy has significant lattice distortion.
The as-synthesized high-entropy nanoalloy has a random distribution of constituent elements.
The proposed low-entropy baseline has more uniform local atomic surroundings than the high-entropy nanoalloy.
The low-entropy baseline has faster diffusion kinetics than the high-entropy nanoalloy.
The low-entropy baseline has a greater tendency toward microstructural evolution and phase segregation at high temperature.
Lattice distortion creates a locally fluctuating energy landscape with varied local activation barriers.
The varied local energy barriers slow atomic diffusion.
Locally fluctuating energy barriers restrict dislocation motion and make it proceed through nanoscale segment detrapping.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses grain growth at high temperature.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation at high temperature.
Sluggish diffusion stabilizes both the structure and chemistry of high-entropy nanoalloys.
After identical high-temperature annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will have lower diffusion coefficients than the low-entropy counterpart.
After identical high-temperature annealing, the high-entropy nanoalloy will exhibit less grain growth than the low-entropy counterpart.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will retain yield strength better than the low-entropy counterpart under high-temperature conditions.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will retain phase integrity better than the low-entropy counterpart under high-temperature conditions.
Strong element segregation at grain boundaries can become the dominant stabilizing phenomenon and limit the prediction.
The prediction becomes less valid near the melting point because diffusion accelerates markedly.
